blockers: Statutory: discretionary programs are created and funded by Congress, and abolishing or converting them requires legislation.

BUILD America 250 Act (H.R. 8870) has cleared committee only; a short-term extension (H.R. 6500) runs to 2026-12-11, and as of 2026-06-05 the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee had not released bill text (later Senate action was not found).
Inference: authorizers of both parties and local governments have historically favored keeping some discretionary programs, which makes a wholesale shift to formulas unlikely.
confidence_reason: The administration's consolidation and formula-conversion proposal and the 2026-09-02 extension were confirmed in the Secretary's letter and the public law, both read for this review. The House committee bill's contents and the absence of a floor vote were not rechecked here.

durability.why: If achieved it would be statutory, so durable; nothing has been enacted, and the administration's reported requests are for consolidation of some programs and one formula conversion.

est_completion.basis: Inference: abolishing discretionary programs needs a new authorization law, the House committee bill keeps many of them, and the administration's own letter adds new discretionary programs while DOT still announces competitive awards.

proposal: The Mandate recommends abolishing DOT's discretionary grant-making processes in favor of formula distributions to the states, or at a minimum consolidating the number of grants, and shifting more transportation financing to user fees and private capital. It also asks the Build America Bureau to keep strict underwriting if its loan program continues.
remaining: Congress would need to enact a reauthorization or other statute that ends or consolidates discretionary programs and shifts funds to state formulas; the House committee bill keeps many discretionary programs and no floor vote has occurred.
Enactment of a long-term reauthorization or another extension before the extension expires on 2026-12-11.

The administration's own request pairs consolidation of some programs and one formula conversion (SS4A) with three new discretionary programs, so a wholesale shift to formulas is not what it has proposed.
Any change to Build America Bureau lending standards that the Mandate describes is a separate step (the 2026-07-22 letter addresses the TIFIA and RRIF credit programs but not Bureau underwriting).

status_summary: No law or DOT action abolishing discretionary grants or converting them to state formulas has been found. Secretary Duffy's letter of 2026-07-22 to Senate committee leaders asks Congress to merge many competitive programs (for example the Bridge Investment Program with the Competitive Highway Bridge Program, several rail, bus and ferry programs, and the Rural, INFRA, Mega and BUILD programs into two multimodal programs), to convert Safe Streets and Roads for All from competitive to formula, and to eliminate the Mass Transit Account; it also proposes three new discretionary programs (Interstate construction, freight bottlenecks, digital infrastructure). The House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee approved the bipartisan BUILD America 250 Act (H.R. 8870, about $580 billion over FY2027 to FY2031) on 2026-05-22 with a larger Bridge Formula Program (alongside a smaller competitive bridge program), a transit consolidated state block grant (urbanized areas may opt out), a new discretionary Surface Transportation Accelerator Grant that a law-firm summary says resembles BUILD and INFRA, and several discretionary programs retained, including Safe Streets and Roads for All (codified as a grant program), INFRA and, per the law-firm summary, Mega and Capital Investment Grants; no floor vote was found. DOT's FY2027 budget request (released 2026-04-03) keeps the core highway program on formulas, funds INFRA and Capital Investment Grants and sets the BUILD line to zero, without proposing a shift of discretionary programs to formulas. H.R. 6500, the Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (Public Law 119-103), was signed on 2026-09-02; its Division C extends surface transportation authority through 2026-12-11, and DOT announced $426 million in INFRA grants on 2026-10-01.

timeline.event: The reconciliation law (Public Law 119-21) is signed; a law-firm summary says it rescinds funding for several transportation grant programs created or funded under prior laws, including most of the Neighborhood Access and Equity Grant Program. This reduces some discretionary funding but does not convert any program to state formulas.

Senate Environment and Public Works Chairman Capito outlines principles for the surface transportation reauthorization: reduce overlapping federal programs, steer more money to highway formula programs states can plan around, and avoid top-down mandates; she also notes a backlog of more than 3,200 awarded discretionary grants without signed agreements. A trade report of 2026-06-05 says EPW had not released bill text and that she remained focused on flexible formula funds to states.

DOT releases its FY2027 budget request documents. The Budget Highlights keep the core Federal-aid Highway Program at $64.7 billion, distributed mainly by formula, request $770 million for INFRA (competitive) and $713.7 million for the Bridge Formula Program, set National Infrastructure Investments (the BUILD line), Rural and Tribal Infrastructure Advancement and the Federal-State Partnership rail line at zero, request $1.2 billion for Capital Investment Grants (down from $1.7 billion in FY2026), and do not propose consolidating surface grant programs or include a reauthorization proposal (release date from DOT's budget page; the Highlights page was last updated 2026-05-05).

A Congressional Research Service report on the FY2027 DOT budget request describes the request as ending the discretionary programs funded by IIJA multiyear advance appropriations and cutting annual appropriations for some others (BUILD and MEGA from $145 million in FY2026 to zero; Capital Investment Grants from $1.7 billion to $1.2 billion). It does not describe any program being converted to formula funding, and it shows the Bridge Formula Program at $714 million, down from $5.5 billion per year under the IIJA.

H.R. 8870, the BUILD America 250 Act, is introduced by Rep. Graves with Reps. Larsen, Rouzer, Webster and Norton as cosponsors and referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee. The introduced text rewrites the bridge program as a formula program (authorized at $9.2 billion a year for FY2027 to FY2031, with a separate $2 billion a year competitive bridge program), creates a transit consolidated state block grant (Sec. 3006), authorizes a Surface Transportation Accelerator Grant (Sec. 1124) and authorizes Safe Streets and Roads for All at $500 million rising to $1 billion (Sec. 1119) (as read from the introduced version; the committee approved an amended bill).

House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee approves the BUILD America 250 Act (H.R. 8870) after a 14-hour markup; the committee's release gives no vote tally and says the chairman plans to bring the bill to the floor soon. The committee's section-by-section summary describes a bridge formula program with set-asides, a transit consolidated state block grant, a pilot letting up to ten states receive their base highway apportionment as a lump sum, a new discretionary Surface Transportation Accelerator Grant, a codified Safe Streets and Roads for All program that remains a grant program, and repeal of several grant programs (for example Neighborhood Access and Equity). A law-firm summary reports a 62-2 vote (other reports give 61-2), about $580 billion over FY2027 to FY2031 ($474.4 billion from the Highway Trust Fund), and some program consolidation (for example three intercity rail programs into one).

Secretary Duffy sends the chairs and ranking members of three Senate committees the administration's surface transportation reauthorization priorities. The letter proposes consolidating many competitive grant programs, converting Safe Streets and Roads for All to a formula program, eliminating the Mass Transit Account, adding three new discretionary programs, and raising the RRIF cap and replenishing private activity bond authority; it does not name the Build America Bureau. Read in full from the PDF as posted by ARTBA; the letter proposes no state block grants and names SS4A as its only explicit conversion to formula, and also proposes dropping the Carbon Reduction competitive program in favor of the CMAQ formula program.
timeline.source: U.S. Department of Transportation (letter as posted by ARTBA)

timeline.event: The President signs H.R. 6500, the Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027, which funds agencies through 2026-12-11 and extends authorities including surface transportation, per the White House statement. The enrolled text on GovInfo shows Division C is the Surface Transportation Extension Act of 2026 (Secs. 3001 to 3201), with appropriations and most extensions running to 2026-12-11 and Highway Trust Fund expenditure authority to 2026-12-12; a Congressional Research Service report of 2026-09-14 identifies the current extension of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act authorizations through 2026-12-11 as P.L. 119-103. A trade report says the House passed it 370-48 on 2026-09-01 after Senate approval. A long-term reauthorization has not been enacted.
DOT announces $426 million in INFRA grants for freight and highway projects in 12 states, showing that DOT continues to award grants under a program it administers by application.

title: Replace DOT discretionary grants with formula distributions to the states
uncertainties: The 2026-07-22 letter was read through a text summary of the PDF (hosted by ARTBA, not DOT), so section-level details such as the SS4A conversion and the program merger lists should be checked against the PDF; the two trade summaries the earlier record relied on do not mention consolidation or the SS4A conversion, which the letter itself contains. Pass 5: the introduced text of H.R. 8870 (GovInfo) and the committee's section-by-section and release were read, but the committee-reported (amended) text and the congress.gov status page were not (congress.gov blocks automated fetches), so the vote count (62-2 per one law-firm summary, 61-2 per other reports) and the absence of a floor vote rest on secondary reports and the committee site; the committee release gives no tally. The White House statement confirms H.R. 6500 was signed on 2026-09-02 and does not give a public law number; the public law text on GovInfo confirms that H.R. 6500 became Public Law 119-103, approved 2026-09-02, with Division C extending surface transportation programs through 2026-12-11. The FY2027 request is described through a CRS report only, and it shows the Bridge Formula Program cut sharply as well as discretionary programs, so it does not read as a shift to formulas. The Senate side is described only through Chairman Capito's 2025-07-16 principles (which favor highway formula programs and cutting overlapping programs, a direction closer to the Mandate than the House committee bill) and a 2026-06-05 trade report; no Senate bill text was found. Not checked: DOT grant-condition changes in 2025, FY2026 appropriations structure, and Build America Bureau lending practices. Stage rests on a legislative request, not an enacted change, and is a judgment since the Mandate's primary recommendation (abolish, use formulas) is broader than the request.
